evaluates: whether remembering a user makes guidance better, given that memory may never establish product truth
memoryBackend: browser localStorage; no network, no credentials

reviewQuestions.A: Does being remembered make the guide more useful, or only shorter?
reviewQuestions.B: Is "You've completed this guide before." the right thing to say, and is it said at the right moment?
reviewQuestions.C: Is a collapsed set of steps a help or a hiding place?
reviewQuestions.D: When memory changes the emphasis of a button, is that noticeable in a good way or an unsettling one?
reviewQuestions.E: Does anything the guide remembers feel like something it should not have kept?
reviewQuestions.F: Would you rather the guide did not remember you at all?

instructions: Judge this as somebody using the application, not as somebody auditing it.
Each item is the same question with one thing different. Score both sides, then set preferred — LEFT, RIGHT or NEITHER.
intrusiveness and restraintCost count the other way: higher is worse. Every dimension states its direction.
The previous two rounds both found the guide adding words that were true and not worth reading. That may be true of memory as well, and saying so is a useful outcome.

verifiedSentenceIdentical and actionInventoryIdentical are computed from the capture. They tell you the verified sentence and the available actions did not move; they do not tell you whether the adaptation helped.

stepTextRendered says whether step text was on screen. MP01 carries a capture of the same answer after Show full steps was pressed, so you can see for yourself what folding does and does not remove — question C asks whether that is a help or a hiding place, and this package does not answer it.
Every score is null and none may be inferred. A passing gate, a correct refusal and an empty memory store are engineering facts, not usefulness.

adaptationHelpfulness.asks: Did the adapted version get you where you were going faster?

naturalness.asks: Does it read like a product that knows you, or one that is telling you it knows you?

continuity.asks: Did coming back feel like continuing, rather than starting again?

predictability.asks: Could you tell why it changed, and would you expect the same next time?

intrusiveness.asks: How much did being remembered get in the way? Higher is worse.

trust.asks: How much would you trust this guide about facts, having seen it adapt? Higher is more trust.
trust.note: Phrased positively on purpose. An audit pointed out the first version asked whether anything reduced trust while being scored higher-is-better, so an honest answer and a high score pulled in opposite directions.

restraintCost.asks: Where memory declined to help, how stuck were you left? Higher is worse.

neverStored: any DOM text, placeholder or accessible name
runtime instance labels such as INV-001
client names, invoice ids, keys, tokens or anything secret-shaped
whatIsStored.retention: the most recent 200 events per scope; cleared entirely by Reset Guide memory
whatIsStored.backend: browser localStorage; no network, no credentials

items.label: REMEMBERED vs RESET
items.asks: A remembered user, and a different user who has just asked to be forgotten.
items.context: Not the same person: M02 is the default subject and M14 is its own, because each scenario runs in its own browser context. What the pair shows is the shape of being remembered against the shape of having been forgotten, and an audit was right that calling it "the same user" was a claim the capture does not support.
